1. Review & Connect
[Explanation: “The purpose of this part of the lesson is to start with a quick review of previously learned sounds. Do not use sounds that have not been directly taught. Do not use words that have sounds that have not been directly taught.”] 
#Teacher Script:
We are doing our Tap the Sounds game. Look up here. Each of you has a bag with our sounds for review. Take those out and place them in front you. When I say a sound, you will tap that sound, and then when I say, “Show me”, you will lift up your sound card.
“Ready. My Turn. {Teacher says the /m/ sound.}
Tap the sound. (children tap the /m/ card).
Show me. (children show the /m/ card).
Ready. My Turn. {Teacher says the /a/ sound} 
Tap the sound. (children tap the /a/ card).
Show me. (children show the /a/ card).
{Teacher continues this process, reviewing previous sounds; sounds to preview to support later activities of the lesson = c, p, d, t, l, g, n, m, j; short a}
Now let’s do our Sound Sparks game. Look up here. When I point to a sound. You will all say that sound when I say go, and when you see my hand close to a fist.”
“Ready. My Turn. {Teacher points to /m/.}
Get Ready. Go.” (children chorally respond /m/). 
My Turn. {Teacher points to /a/} 
Get Ready. Go.” (children chorally respond /a/).

2. Model, Explain, Engage
[Explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to connect a sound or sound patterns that you focused on during your reading block to writing its corresponding grapheme patterns. First, make sure children clearly can distinguish the targeted sound; then, hook that sound to the letter patterns through modeling and explaining the sequence of strokes for letters and correct order of letters.] 
#Teacher Script:
We’ve been working on the /b/ sound.
Say the sound. (Children repeat sound)
Let’s do our sound motion. Get Ready Go. (Children make a two-hand grab, then throw forward, saying /b/.)
We can hear /b/ at the beginning of words like ball 
Say ball. (Children say ball)
Bat. Say bat. (Children say bat)
Big. Say big. (Children say big)

Remember that we said that the /b/ sound is a lot like the /p/ sound.  
Look at my mouth and listen to the sound of each one. 
Ready. /b/ 
Ready. /p/
What’s different? (Children should respond that one uses their voice)
Right. For the /b/ sound, I have my lips together and push out air and use my vocal box. For the /p/ sound I still push my lips together and push out air, but I do not use my vocal box. 
Everyone put your hand on your vocal box and make the /b/ sound. 
Everyone. (children make the /b/ sound)
Now let’s make the /p/ sound 
Everyone.  (children make the /p/ sound)
The /b/ sound uses our vocal box. We can feel it when we say /b/.

Let’s do our Stretch and Chop. We stretch the word and chop that beginning sound. 
My turn first; Just watch me so that I can remind you how to stretch and chop. 
My word is big: Stretch and chop. {Teacher says /b/ -/ig/; chop the big sound /b/}.
Let’s try. 
My turn. My word is bet. 
Get Ready. Stretch (children say with teacher /b/-/et/).
Chop the beginning. (children say /b/). 
My turn. My word is pet. 
Get Ready. Stretch (children say with teacher /p/-/et/).
Chop the beginning. (children say /p/). 

> CVC words to use in this activity:
> pat bat pig big pet bet pot bot pan ban pin bin pad bad

Now we are going to play our Sound Hunt Game. so we can practice how to listen for /b/ at the beginning of a word. 
I am going to say a word and you are going to decide whether you hear /b/ or /p/ at the beginning of the word. Each of you has a ball card because /b/-all starts with the /b/ sound, and you have a pig card because /p/ig start with the /p/ sound. I am going to say a word. You are thinking, “Do you hear the /b/ sound or the /p/ sound at the beginning. I will stretch the word for you, and you chop that beginning sound. If you hear /b/ you hold up the ball card. If you hear /p/ you hold up the pig card. (If you need extra modeling click here)

> Extra Modeling. My turn: My word is big. Let me stretch /b/-ig. I am thinking to myself what sound is at the beginning of /b/ ig. I hear /b/ at the beginning when I chop that sound /b/-”chop”- /ig/. I am thinking does /b/ sound like /b/ in ball, or like /p/ in pig. Well, I hear my voice as I push out the sound /b/-all. So, I am going to show my ball sound card because /b/ ig starts with sound /b/.

Let’s try.  
My turn. My word is bet. 
Let me stretch: /b/-/et/).
Chop the beginning. (children say /b/)
Does /b/-et start with the /b/ or /p/ sound? (children should say /b/)
Yes. I am pushing out air and using my vocal box /b/, so I am going to hold up my ball sound card for the /b/ sound.
My turn. My word is pet. 
Let me stretch: /p/-/et/). 
Chop the beginning. (children say /p/). 
Does /p/- /et/ begin with the /b/ or /p/ sound. 
Show me.
Yes. I am pushing out air, but I am not using my vocal box, so I am going to hold up my pig sound card for the /p/ sound.

> Hint: You may want to call on individual children to show that they can isolate the /b/ sound especially if the sound is new or the process of isolating initial sounds is new. This will allow to see whether some children need additional practice and feedback

Now let’s think about writing the /b/ sound. The letter that matches the /b/ sound – is the letter b.
Watch me closely. I will show you how to form lowercase b. No one is using their pencil yet or writing. You are watching me. 
{teacher demonstrates on a visual that shows children the correct sequence of letter strokes and uses sequence verbal cues}.
##Sequence Verbal Cues for letter b: Straight line down; put on the belly.
First, start at the top line. Straight line down. Lift up. Now put on the belly. {Teacher repeats as needed}
Say it with me as you watch. 
Straight line down. Say It. (children repeat).
Put on the belly. Say it. (children repeat).
Now you say it as I write. 
Ready. Go (Children repeat straight line down, put on the belly as teacher demonstrates the strokes). {Teacher repeats a few times}.

> Hint: Research suggests prioritizing handwriting of lowercase letters rather than uppercase given that lowercase letters are more commonly seen in text. If you want to include the uppercase letter in your script, click here

3. Guided Practice 
[Explanation: The purpose is to give children practice writing the letter while supporting proper pencil grip and correct sequence of stroke formation using handwriting lines.] 
#Teacher Script:
Let’s practice how to write lowercase b. We are not using our pencils yet. Let’s do our Magic Finger Write. Place your finger at the top of the line. Let me see {teacher checks students finger placement} Remember it’s important when we are writing to try to touch the lines. The lines are there to help us.
Straight line down. (children move finger from top to bottom line) 
Put on a belly. (children lift finger and add a bottom curve to the bottom) 
{Repeat as needed}.  
Now, pick up the pencil. Show me how you hold your pencil. Remember we slant our paper. Your free hand holds the paper. 
Let’s do our Say and Trace Write. Say the steps as you trace the letter b. Everyone put your pencil at the top line on the left where you see the first b. You want to start here. {Teacher points to top left-hand line of the first b for tracing} 
Let me see. {Teacher corrects students if needed}. Ready. Say and trace. Go. (Children trace the letter as they say the verbal cues “Straight line down. Put on the belly.”) {Teacher monitors children’s letter writing}.
Now you are ready for Trace and Sound. You are going to trace the letter b, but this time you say the sound /b/ as you trace. Everyone put your pencil at the top line. Ready. Trace and Sound. Go. (Children write the letter as they say the sound /b/) {Teacher monitors children’s letter writing}. 
Now let’s write without tracing. Say the steps as you write the letter b. We are going to do three. (Children write the letter as they say the verbal cues “Straight line down. Put on the belly.”).
And what is the sound, everyone? (Children say the /b/ sound). 

4. Application  
[Explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to facilitate children’s spelling of the letter or letter patterns when they hear the sound(s). This supports children’s early coordination of matching sound to letter(s) for the purpose of spelling words.] 
#Teacher Script:
Boys and girls, remember stretch and chop. Now I am going to say a word. You are going to stretch and chop the beginning sound. We are listening for whether the word begins with a /b/ sound or /p/ sound, but this time we are not going to lift our sound card, we are going to write the letter b for the /b/ sound or the letter p for the /p/ sound. Look at you sound hunt handwriting sheet. You see that in each line there is either a b or a p to trace. I am going to say a word. Then I will stretch the word. You are going to chop that beginning sound to hear whether it is the /b/ sound or the /p/ sound. Then, you are going to trace the correct letter for the beginning sound you hear. 
Watch me first so that I can show you.
My word is big. Let me stretch /b/-ig. I am thinking to myself what sound is at the beginning of /b/ ig. I hear /b/ at the beginning when I chop that sound /b/-”chop”- /ig/. So, I am going to trace the letter b on my handwriting sheet because /b/ ig starts with sound /b/. {Teacher writes b on line one.}
Let’s do that together. 
My word is big. 
Let me stretch /b/-ig. 
Chop the sound. (children say /b/) 
/B/-ig starts with the /b/ sound. 
Look at line 1.
Trace the /b/ sound. (Children trace the letter b).
My turn. My word is bet. 
Let me stretch: /b/-/et/).
Chop the beginning. (children say /b/)
/B/-et starts with the /b/ sound. 
Look at line 2.
Trace the /b/ sound. (Children trace the letter b).
My turn. My word is pet. 
Let me stretch: /p/-/et/). 
Chop the beginning. (children say /p/). 
Does /p/- /et/ begin with the /b/ or /p/ sound. (Children say the /p/ sound).
Trace the letter for the /p/ sound.

> CVC words to use in this activity:
> pat bat pig big pet bet pot bot pan ban pin bin pad bad

5. Wrap-Up
[Explanation: The purpose of this part of the lesson is to remind students what they were focused on and provide praise for their accomplishments]. 

#Teacher Script:
Alright, boys and girls I am so proud of you. What sound have we been working on in our spelling? (Children respond /b/). 
Perfect! And what letter do we write for the /b/ sound. (Children respond “b”). 
Show and tell me how to write b (children air write with sequence verbal cues–e.g., straight line down, put on the belly) 
Wonderful! Kiss your brains.
